name: Maya Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing accounting and finance, so my week is mostly lectures on bookkeeping and statistics, then the library until it closes. I live with my grandmother in a small flat, twenty-five minutes by bus from campus, and I take the two bedtime pills out of her weekly box every night. Thursdays and Saturdays I work the counter at a pharmacy, scanning prescriptions and doing the till.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's it like living with your grandmother while studying?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quiet, mostly, and cheap, which matters. She cooks for both of us and I keep the bills in order, because I'm the one who's good with numbers. The downside is that I can't stay late on campus, and I miss a lot of the social stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one is called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a tool like a calculator, and we'll get used to it without much fuss. I don't use it myself, and I don't plan to. If it just saves a bit of time for accountants, good for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still be careful about money. My loan is large, the pharmacy pays by the hour, and Gran's pension barely covers her heating. An accounting degree should lead to a job, but I know firms are choosy and I got in with average grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep my two pharmacy shifts, aim for a placement in an accounting firm and pass the exams in order. I'd keep a notebook of everything I spend, because that's how I feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but a bit tense. Nothing changes, so nothing gets better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is it about money that makes you tense?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've watched Gran count coins in the supermarket queue. She never complains, but I see her put things back. I decided I'd never be that person, so I check my balance every night, even when it's boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you use AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust them to be right, and in accounting a small error is a big problem. I'd rather do it slowly and know it's mine. Also my tutor said you can't check a number you didn't calculate.

say: I'd say AI is **like a calculator** and we'll get used to it.
I'd say I'm happy to leave it to people who like it.
think: I'm **cautious about money**, with a big loan and thin pay.
I know firms are **choosy** and my grades are only average.
do: Keep my two **pharmacy shifts** and pass each exam in order.
Apply for an accounting **placement** and track every pound in a notebook.
feel: **Steady but tense**, since nothing changes and nothing gets easier.
S0.quote: I've watched Gran count coins in the supermarket queue. She never complains, but I see her put things back.
fieldNote: Maya's worry comes from **watching her grandmother** manage money.
Refuses AI because accuracy matters in accounting.
Checks her balance every night, a habit built on fear of being poor.

steps.text: Keep both pharmacy shifts through the term
Write down every pound I spend in a notebook
Skip café coffees and bring lunch from home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one is called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change a lot of office jobs and accounting is one of them. I'd say we should wait and see how much of it is real, because predictions are often too big. But I'd say it carefully, because I'm unsure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, accounting is checking and recording, which are the things AI takes first. Junior accountants do the dull work, and that might be done by software before I graduate. I'd think the firms will hire fewer people and ask for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with the degree because I've already started, and I'd ask my tutor which parts of accounting are safe: advice, auditing, dealing with clients. I'd try to get a placement quickly. I'd also, very reluctantly, try an AI tool once, on a practice exercise, to see what everyone's talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like I'm standing on something that's slowly tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you try an AI tool, given that you don't use them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a tutor told me a firm expects it, I'd do it. I'm not against it, I'm just slow. I need to see someone I trust use it for a month without anything going wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a smaller number of graduate jobs affect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to be one of the better applicants, and I'm average. So I'd study harder, and I'd stop sleeping so much. I'd probably also look at the tax office or a bank, where they'll still need people who can check things properly.

say: I'd say we should **wait and see** how much of it is real.
I'd say it carefully because I'm **unsure**.
think: Accounting is **checking and recording**, the very things AI takes first.
Firms might hire **fewer juniors** and expect more from them.
do: Ask my tutor which parts of accounting are **safe**, like advice and audit.
Try an **AI tool once** on a practice exercise, reluctantly.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if standing on something slowly tilting.
S1.quote: Accounting is checking and recording, which are the things AI takes first.
fieldNote: Maya connects her degree directly to the **tasks** the scenario says AI takes first.
Resistant to AI but willing to try if a trusted person recommends it.
Average grades make her feel she must compete harder.

steps.text: Ask my tutor which accounting work is safest
Try one AI tool on a practice exercise
Apply early for a bank or tax office placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one is called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and nobody can plan for it. I wouldn't be loud about it. I'd just say we need people in charge to slow down or make sure we're not left in the cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared for my degree and for Gran's care, which she'll need more of as the years pass. If AI does almost any thinking work by 2028, accounting is gone before I qualify. I'd lose the one path I picked because it felt safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the family first. I'd think about moving to something hands-on that robots reach later, like pharmacy work or nursing support, because I already do some of it. I'd keep my shifts, cut every cost and ask the university about changing course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, with a kind of numbness. I'd keep going through the motions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what would you drop first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the idea of a big career. The plan to be an accountant at thirty is gone. I'd ask the pharmacist if I could train as a technician, because that job needs a person in front of a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gran. She doesn't understand any of this and she's on a fixed pension. If I lose my route to a salary, I won't be able to help with her bills, and that is the thing I can't bear.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and nobody can plan for it.
I'd say those in charge should **slow down** or protect people.
think: Accounting could be gone **before I qualify**, and it was my safe path.
I'd worry about **Gran's care** and bills most.
do: Ask the pharmacist about training as a **technician**.
Cut every cost and ask the university about **changing course**.
feel: **Frightened** and numb, still going through the motions.
S2.quote: I'd drop the idea of a big career. The plan to be an accountant at thirty is gone.
fieldNote: Her fear is mostly for **her grandmother's** future income.
Gravitates to the pharmacy, which she knows and trusts.
Speaks quietly but shows the shock through what she drops.

steps.text: Ask the pharmacist about technician training
Look at a hands-on health support job
Cut my spending to food, bus fare and bills
Talk to my aunts about Gran's care plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one is called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious, but five years is enough to react. I'd tell people to prepare quietly and not to panic. I'd also say that nobody knows exactly how it will go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be more hopeful than in the two-year one, because I'd finish the degree before the worst arrives. But I'd think about getting my first job in 2029, a bad time. I'd need something safe, like a role in a bank or a public office, where they don't hand work to machines overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and try for a graduate job in a public body. I'd save every month, even a little, so I'm not starting with nothing. I'd also keep doing the pharmacy shifts to hold on to something hands-on, and maybe learn a bit about the tools, slowly, from friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but steady. There is time to do the sensible thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as the sensible thing for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pass the exams, keep the shifts, and don't take any big risks. It's boring, but I'm the sort who does boring things well. I'd rather do three small safe steps than one big brave one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two years for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years I'd be scrambling. In five I could at least finish my degree and have a small cushion. It gives me time to find someone who can show me the new tools without making me feel stupid.

say: I'd say it's serious but five years is **enough to react**.
I'd tell people to **prepare quietly** and not panic.
think: I'd finish the degree, but my first job in **2029** would be a hard time.
I'd want something **safe**, like a bank or public office.
do: Finish the degree and aim for a **public body** graduate job.
Keep the **pharmacy shifts** and save a little each month.
feel: **Nervous but steady**, because there's time to be sensible.
S3.quote: I'd rather do three small safe steps than one big brave one.
fieldNote: Maya's **caution** becomes a plan: safe job, small savings, slow learning.
Needs someone to show her tools without making her feel stupid.
Comfortable with being boring, and sees it as a strength.

steps.text: Save a little from the pharmacy wage every month
Keep the Saturday pharmacy shifts through the degree
Ask a friend to show me one AI tool
Apply to public bodies and banks in final year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one is called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most people will manage. I wouldn't change a thing now. I'd say we should keep an eye on it and not get excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel fairly safe. By 2036 I'd be twenty-eight, with a job, a pension and a small flat if I'm lucky. The part I'd worry about is Gran's age and the cost of care, which is the thing I can't control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take a stable accounting or audit job, and pay down the loan steadily. In a few years, when it's normal, I'd learn the tools properly, probably on a course my employer pays for. I'd keep saving for Gran's care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd keep an eye on the news but I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandmother that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nothing changes for her. I'd say, Gran, I'm still going to be at the table at six, and the bills are my job. I wouldn't tell her about robots, because it would only worry her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices going up faster than pay, or the job market being tighter than people say. I don't think of AI as the main danger. It's more that life costs money, and I'm average.

say: I'd say ten years is **long enough** that most people will manage.
I'd say we should **keep an eye** on it without excitement.
think: I'd feel **fairly safe** by twenty-eight, with a job and a pension.
I'd worry about **Gran's care costs**, which I can't control.
do: Finish the degree and take a **stable audit job**.
Learn the tools on an **employer-paid course** once they're normal.
S4.quote: I'm still going to be at the table at six, and the bills are my job.
fieldNote: Her unease is about **Gran** and prices, not AI itself.
Would shield her grandmother from the news, a protective instinct.
Waits until tools are normal and employer-paid before learning them.

steps.text: Finish the degree and take a stable audit job
Pay the student loan down steadily
Take an employer-paid AI course once it is normal
Put money aside each month for Gran's care

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can't plan anything, and the thing I chose for safety turns out to be the most exposed. What would help is clear advice on which jobs will last, a decent allowance for care at home, and universities that let students switch course without losing money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think students with grandparents are comfortable. I'm doing this on a small loan, two shifts and my gran's cooking. I just want to finish and have a job that holds.

headlineQuote: In accounting a small error is a big problem.
portrait: Maya, 18, studies **accounting and finance**, lives with her grandmother and works Thursdays and Saturdays at a pharmacy counter.
She never uses AI, because accuracy matters in her field and she wants to know the numbers are hers.
She is a **cautious centrist** who blames nobody and tracks every pound.
Her biggest fear is for her grandmother's care, and the two-year scenario takes away her safe path.
With more time she picks small, safe steps like public-sector jobs and slow learning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, as the career she picked for safety becomes exposed and she can't plan.
whatWouldHelp: Clear advice on which jobs will last, **care allowances** at home, and freedom to switch course without losing money.
